hints: Focus on the definition of a chiral centre, a carbon with four different groups attached to it.
Look closely at X, it is bonded to H, OH, the C=O group above and the rest of the chain below.
Now compare Y with Z, check which one has two identical H atoms and so cannot be chiral.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes a carbon chiral**

A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.

Rule to use:
$$\text{chiral C = C bonded to 4 different groups, no double bonds, no two identical groups}$$

**Check carbon X**

X is $\text{HO}-\text{C}-\text{H}$. Its four bonds are to $-\text{OH}$, $-\text{H}$, $-\text{C=O}$ above, and $-\text{CH(OH)}-$ below.

All four groups are different, so X is a chiral centre.

**Check carbon Y**

Y is $\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{OH}$. Its four bonds are to $-\text{H}$, $-\text{OH}$, the longer chain above, and the shorter chain below ending in $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

The up and down chains are different, so all four groups are different and Y is a chiral centre.

**Check carbon Z and conclude**

Z is $\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{H}$ with $-\text{OH}$ below. It is a $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group.

Because it has two identical H atoms, it cannot be chiral. So only X and Y are chiral centres.

options.A: Incorrect. While X and Y are chiral, Z is $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ with two H atoms attached. A carbon with two identical groups can never be a chiral centre.
options.B: Correct. Both X and Y are $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbons bonded to H, OH, and two different chain fragments above and below. Z is $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ with two H atoms, so it is achiral.
options.C: Incorrect. X is indeed chiral, but Y is also chiral. Y has H, OH, and two different carbon chains on either side, so it should not be left out.
options.D: Incorrect. Y is chiral, but X is also chiral for the same reason. Both have four different groups, so choosing only one misses the other chiral centre.
